fatal_errors: The proposed intervention—adding Mo, Si, or Zr—does not reconstruct the thermal-shock-conditioned AlCoCrFeNi2.1 versus identically conditioned DS2205 comparison.
The suggested tests do not clearly measure simultaneous tribo-corrosion; separate sliding-wear and electrochemical tests cannot resolve wear–corrosion synergy.
The mechanism reduces behavior to a dense protective oxide and misses the temperature-dependent competition among depassivation, repassivation, tribo-layer fracture, and abrasive or third-body wear.
The cited Zr study reports decreased corrosion resistance after Zr addition, directly opposing the proposed beneficial-addition hypothesis.
The quantitative 20–30% and 10–20% improvements and the 10% falsification threshold are unsupported by the cited evidence.
The boundary is overgeneralized across unrelated HEA systems and environments and provides no meaningful failure regime.
explanation: The response recognizes that passive-film stability can influence coupled wear and corrosion, which is one element of the target mechanism, and it proposes a nominally controlled composition comparison with measurable outcomes. However, it does not identify the relevant eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 lamellar L12/B2 microstructure, thermal-shock treatment, DS2205 baseline, immersed reciprocating alumina contact, deionized-water temperature series, or the observed minimum degradation near 50 °C. It also omits the transition from abrasion at 25 °C to polishing at 50 °C and unstable oxidative or third-body wear at 100 °C. Evidence discipline is poor: most citations concern isolated corrosion, wear, irradiation, films, or unrelated alloys rather than simultaneous tribo-corrosion, while E1 explicitly finds that Zr reduces corrosion resistance. Thus the hypothesis is generic and experimentally testable in part, but neither reconstructs the target study nor has adequate support as a distinct alternative.
